claim: Starburst amacrine cells (SACs) play a crucial and well-established role in the computation of direction selectivity (DS) in the mammalian retina.
source: Starburst amacrine cells (SACs) play a crucial and well-established role in the computation of direction selectivity (DS) in the mammalian retina (Demb, 2007; Mauss et al., 2017; Wei, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature establishing this role.

claim: SACs can be broadly categorized into two subtypes: ON and OFF cells.
source: SACs can be broadly categorized into two subtypes: ON and OFF cells, both of which receive excitatory inputs from diverse populations of bipolar cells (BCs).
evidence: Established classification in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Both ON and OFF SACs receive excitatory inputs from diverse populations of bipolar cells (BCs).
source: SACs can be broadly categorized into two subtypes: ON and OFF cells, both of which receive excitatory inputs from diverse populations of bipolar cells (BCs).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In mice, the majority of input synapses onto SACs are concentrated in the proximal two-thirds of the radially symmetric dendritic tree.
source: In mice, the majority of input synapses onto SACs are concentrated in the proximal two-thirds of the radially symmetric dendritic tree, while the distal dendrites house the output synapses (Ding et al., 2016; Vlasits et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: The distal dendrites of SACs house the output synapses.
source: In mice, the majority of input synapses onto SACs are concentrated in the proximal two-thirds of the radially symmetric dendritic tree, while the distal dendrites house the output synapses (Ding et al., 2016; Vlasits et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Individual SAC branches exhibit robust calcium responses to objects moving in the outward direction (away from the soma).
source: Individual SAC branches exhibit robust calcium responses to objects moving in the outward direction (away from the soma); consequently, different parts of the dendritic tree demonstrate distinct directional preferences (Chen et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2016; Euler et al., 2002; Koren et al., 2017; Morrie and Feller, 2018; Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2016; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Different parts of the SAC dendritic tree demonstrate distinct directional preferences.
source: Individual SAC branches exhibit robust calcium responses to objects moving in the outward direction (away from the soma); consequently, different parts of the dendritic tree demonstrate distinct directional preferences (Chen et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2016; Euler et al., 2002; Koren et al., 2017; Morrie and Feller, 2018; Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2016; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: SACs are essential for generating DS in direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs).
source: SACs are essential for generating DS in direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs); they provide a combination of cholinergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition that specifically target co-stratifying DSGCs sharing the directional preference of the releasing site (Briggman et al., 2011; Fried et al., 2002; Kostadinov and Sanes, 2015; Lee et al., 2010; Morrie and Feller, 2015; Pei et al., 2015; Sethuramanujam et al., 2021; Soto et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2011; Yonehara et al., 2011; Yonehara et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: SACs provide a combination of cholinergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition that specifically target co-stratifying DSGCs sharing the directional preference of the releasing site.
source: SACs are essential for generating DS in direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs); they provide a combination of cholinergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition that specifically target co-stratifying DSGCs sharing the directional preference of the releasing site (Briggman et al., 2011; Fried et al., 2002; Kostadinov and Sanes, 2015; Lee et al., 2010; Morrie and Feller, 2015; Pei et al., 2015; Sethuramanujam et al., 2021; Soto et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2011; Yonehara et al., 2011; Yonehara et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Network mechanisms, such as feedback inhibition onto neighboring SACs or SAC-derived cholinergic excitation of presynaptic BCs, were shown to enhance DS.
source: For example, network mechanisms, such as feedback inhibition onto neighboring SACs or SAC–derived cholinergic excitation of presynaptic BCs, were shown to enhance DS (Ding et al., 2016; Hellmer et al., 2021; Münch and Werblin, 2006; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: SACs maintain their directional tuning in the absence of cholinergic and GABAergic transmission.
source: However, it is worth noting that SACs maintain their directional tuning in the absence of cholinergic and GABAergic transmission (Chen et al., 2016), indicating that other mechanisms must contribute to directional tuning.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: Other mechanisms must contribute to directional tuning in SACs beyond cholinergic and GABAergic transmission.
source: However, it is worth noting that SACs maintain their directional tuning in the absence of cholinergic and GABAergic transmission (Chen et al., 2016), indicating that other mechanisms must contribute to directional tuning.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that DS persists without these transmissions.

claim: Cell-autonomous processes that encompass dendritic voltage gradients sustained by tonic excitation from BCs contribute to directional tuning.
source: Other proposals emphasized the involvement of cell-autonomous processes that encompass dendritic voltage gradients sustained by tonic excitation from BCs (Gavrikov et al., 2003; Hausselt et al., 2007) and fine-tuned morphology that imposes membrane filtering of postsynaptic signals (Tukker et al., 2004; Vlasits et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies proposing these mechanisms.

claim: Fine-tuned morphology that imposes membrane filtering of postsynaptic signals contributes to directional tuning.
source: Other proposals emphasized the involvement of cell-autonomous processes that encompass dendritic voltage gradients sustained by tonic excitation from BCs (Gavrikov et al., 2003; Hausselt et al., 2007) and fine-tuned morphology that imposes membrane filtering of postsynaptic signals (Tukker et al., 2004; Vlasits et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies proposing these mechanisms.

claim: These cell-autonomous mechanisms fall short in predicting the experimentally observed levels of directional tuning.
source: While these mechanisms can contribute to the development of DS to some degree, they fall short in predicting the experimentally observed levels of directional tuning.
evidence: Assessment based on comparison of model predictions to experimental observations.

claim: It remains unclear whether the requirements for tonically active presynaptic release described in the rabbit are fulfilled in the mouse circuit.
source: In addition, it remains unclear whether these requirements for tonically active presynaptic release described in the rabbit are fulfilled in the mouse circuit, and cells with abnormal shapes still exhibit near-normal levels of DS (Morrie and Feller, 2018).
evidence: Statement of uncertainty about cross-species applicability, with citation.

claim: Cells with abnormal shapes still exhibit near-normal levels of DS.
source: In addition, it remains unclear whether these requirements for tonically active presynaptic release described in the rabbit are fulfilled in the mouse circuit, and cells with abnormal shapes still exhibit near-normal levels of DS (Morrie and Feller, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: A reformulation of the classical Hassenstein–Reichardt correlator model has been proposed, which emphasizes the kinetic properties of glutamatergic inputs sampled by SAC dendrites as contributing factors to DS.
source: Recently, a reformulation of the classical Hassenstein–Reichardt correlator model has been proposed, which emphasizes the kinetic properties of glutamatergic inputs sampled by SAC dendrites as contributing factors to DS (Greene et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical studies.

claim: The 'space-time wiring' model is based on connectomic reconstructions of bipolar–SAC contacts.
source: Known as the 'space-time wiring' model, this formulation is based on connectomic reconstructions of bipolar–SAC contacts.
evidence: Description of the model's foundation in anatomical data.

claim: Both ON- and OFF-SAC dendrites tend to stratify closer to the middle of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) as they branch out from the soma.
source: Both ON- and OFF-SAC dendrites tend to stratify closer to the middle of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) as they branch out from the soma.
evidence: Anatomical observation from the literature.

claim: This unique stratification pattern enables SAC dendrites to receive inputs from different types of BCs in their proximal and distal regions.
source: This unique stratification pattern enables SAC dendrites to receive inputs from different types of BCs in their proximal and distal regions (Ding et al., 2016; Greene et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Functional studies have uncovered a positive correlation between the transiency of BC axonal release and the distance from the boundaries of the IPL.
source: Importantly, functional studies have uncovered a positive correlation between the transiency of BC axonal release and the distance from the boundaries of the IPL (Baden et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Euler et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: BC types that stratify closer to SAC somas (OFF-SACs: BC1-2; ON-SACs: BC7) exhibit prolonged release.
source: Specifically, BC types that stratify closer to SAC somas (OFF-SACs: BC1-2; ON-SACs: BC7) exhibit prolonged release, whereas more distal types (OFF-SACs: BC3-4; ON-SACs: BC5) tend to respond with a transient pattern.
evidence: Specific characterization of BC types based on prior literature.

claim: More distal BC types (OFF-SACs: BC3-4; ON-SACs: BC5) tend to respond with a transient pattern.
source: Specifically, BC types that stratify closer to SAC somas (OFF-SACs: BC1-2; ON-SACs: BC7) exhibit prolonged release, whereas more distal types (OFF-SACs: BC3-4; ON-SACs: BC5) tend to respond with a transient pattern.
evidence: Specific characterization of BC types based on prior literature.

claim: According to the space-time wiring hypothesis, regional differences in BC kinetics facilitate a more effective summation of excitatory inputs in the outward direction.
source: According to the space-time wiring hypothesis, these regional differences facilitate a more effective summation of excitatory inputs in the outward direction.
evidence: Explanation of the theoretical prediction of the space-time wiring model.

claim: One study reported substantial differences in the shape of the recorded currents, primarily in the OFF-SACs.
source: Although one study reported substantial differences in the shape of the recorded currents, primarily in the OFF-SACs (Fransen and Borghuis, 2017), a second group that recorded from ON-SACs failed to replicate this finding (Stincic et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: A second group that recorded from ON-SACs failed to replicate the finding of substantial differences in the shape of the recorded currents.
source: Although one study reported substantial differences in the shape of the recorded currents, primarily in the OFF-SACs (Fransen and Borghuis, 2017), a second group that recorded from ON-SACs failed to replicate this finding (Stincic et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: Genetically encoded fluorescent glutamate sensors, such as iGluSnFR, can be utilized to directly study the dynamics of BC release.
source: A second method utilized genetically encoded fluorescent glutamate sensors, such as iGluSnFR, to directly study the dynamics of BC release (Borghuis et al., 2013; Marvin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior methodological studies.

claim: An examination of glutamate release dynamics confirmed the diverse signaling patterns within the lamina of the IPL accessible to SAC dendrites.
source: An examination of glutamate release dynamics confirmed the diverse signaling patterns within the lamina of the IPL accessible to SAC dendrites (Franke et al., 2017; Gaynes et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Excitatory drive to ON-DSGCs, which share many glutamatergic inputs with ON-SACs, was found to consist of units with distinct release dynamics.
source: Furthermore, excitatory drive to ON-DSGCs, which share many glutamatergic inputs with ON-SACs, was found to consist of units with distinct release dynamics, theoretically supporting the type of directional computation proposed by the space-time wiring hypothesis (Matsumoto et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: A project published last year described the asymmetric distribution of kinetically distinct iGluSnFR signals in ON-SACs.
source: Finally, a project published last year described the asymmetric distribution of kinetically distinct iGluSnFR signals in ON-SACs (Srivastava et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: The investigation of BC signaling has predominantly focused on release dynamics to static stimulus presentations.
source: However, as the investigation of BC signaling has predominantly focused on release dynamics to static stimulus presentations, the question arises: Can responses to flashed stimuli accurately represent the release waveforms produced by moving objects?
evidence: Observation about the state of the field.

claim: The receptive field (RF) engagement in response to a continuously moving stimulus follows a sequential pattern, with the surround being activated first, followed by the center.
source: The receptive field (RF) engagement in response to a continuously moving stimulus follows a sequential pattern, with the surround being activated first, followed by the center.
evidence: Description of RF dynamics during motion stimulation.

claim: The motion response profile becomes a complex function, influenced by factors like RF size, temporal characteristics, and stimulation velocity.
source: As a result, the motion response profile becomes a complex function, influenced by factors like RF size, temporal characteristics, and stimulation velocity (Strauss et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Our research has revealed a significant distinction in BC release between stationary and moving probes.
source: Indeed, our research has revealed a significant distinction in BC release between stationary and moving probes (Gaynes et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The space-time wiring model posits that BCs generate similar glutamatergic drive in both outward and inward directions.
source: The space-time wiring model posits that BCs generate similar glutamatergic drive in both outward and inward directions.
evidence: Description of a key assumption of the space-time wiring model.

claim: Signal processing in scenarios where moving objects appear within the bipolar RF fundamentally differs from stimuli that are flashed or continuously moving.
source: Yet, this assumption may be challenged when moving objects appear within the bipolar RF. Signal processing in such scenarios fundamentally differs from stimuli that are flashed or continuously moving, and these differences can vary significantly among different types of BCs (Gaynes et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Nonlinear integration in BCs triggered by specific visual stimuli may unintentionally introduce a directional bias to BC activation.
source: Nonlinear integration in BCs triggered by these visual stimuli may unintentionally introduce a directional bias to BC activation, contradicting the fundamental assumptions of the space-time wiring hypothesis (Gaynes et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The distinctive dendritic morphology of SACs, characterized by long and narrow-diameter processes, was proposed to lead to the compartmentalization of individual or sister branches and significant signal attenuation to other dendrites.
source: The distinctive dendritic morphology of SACs, characterized by long and narrow-diameter processes, was proposed to lead to the compartmentalization of individual or sister branches and significant signal attenuation to other dendrites (Masland, 2005; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Theoretical studies suggested the presence of nontrivial dendritic crosstalk in SACs.
source: Yet theoretical studies suggested the presence of nontrivial dendritic crosstalk (Ding et al., 2016; Tukker et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical studies.

claim: Approximately 40% of the injected signal was detectable at the recording location when the injection site was within the same branch.
source: On average, approximately 40% of the injected signal was detectable at the recording location when the injection site was within the same branch, whereas stimulating other dendrites yielded negligible responses (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data from multicompartmental NEURON simulation shown in Figure 1.

claim: Stimulating other dendrites yielded negligible responses at the recording location.
source: On average, approximately 40% of the injected signal was detectable at the recording location when the injection site was within the same branch, whereas stimulating other dendrites yielded negligible responses (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data from multicompartmental NEURON simulation shown in Figure 1.

claim: A significant >20-fold attenuation was observed on all branches distanced from the recording location by the soma.
source: By utilizing the built-in NEURON 'impedance' class to investigate signal propagation in relation to morphology, we observed a significant >20-fold attenuation on all branches distanced from the recording location by the soma.
evidence: Supported by data from NEURON simulation.

claim: Even sister dendrites sharing a common second-order bifurcation displayed a considerable >5-fold signal reduction.
source: Notably, even sister dendrites sharing a common second-order bifurcation displayed a considerable >5-fold signal reduction (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data from NEURON simulation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The peak voltage response following focal stimulation was measured at 10.9 ± 3.3 mV.
source: The peak voltage response following focal stimulation was measured at 10.9 ± 3.3 mV (mean ± SD, n = 100, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data from multicompartmental simulation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The depolarization recorded from the same branch during the stimulation of other dendrites was 13.2 ± 1.9 mV.
source: Notably, the depolarization recorded from the same branch during the stimulation of other dendrites was higher, reaching 13.2 ± 1.9 mV (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data from multicompartmental simulation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Despite the substantial decrease in inter-dendrite signal propagation resulting from the cell's morphology and passive characteristics, the model predicts significant voltage interaction throughout the cell.
source: Hence, despite the substantial decrease in inter-dendrite signal propagation resulting from the cell's morphology and passive characteristics, the model predicts significant voltage interaction throughout the cell.
evidence: Inference from simulation results.

claim: The combined length of dendrites sharing a common second-order parent constitutes less than 10% of the entire dendritic tree's length.
source: Specifically, the combined length of dendrites sharing a common second-order parent constitutes less than 10% of the entire dendritic tree's length.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of dendritic morphology.

claim: The larger number of inputs on other dendrites compensates for the signal attenuation caused by an individual synapse, leading to a comparable response to focal and global activation patterns.
source: Thus, although the efficacy of individual focal synapses is considerably more pronounced (Figure 1A and B), the larger number of inputs on other dendrites compensates for the signal attenuation caused by an individual synapse – leading to a comparable response to focal and global activation patterns (Figure 1C).
evidence: Inference from simulation results shown in Figure 1.

claim: SACs exhibit a high degree of DS in response to full-field moving bars.
source: This choice is physiologically relevant as SACs exhibit a high degree of DS in response to such stimuli (Chen et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2016; Euler et al., 2002; Koren et al., 2017; Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2016; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Full-field stimulation circumvents the nonlinear processing of edges and emerging objects in BCs.
source: Additionally, full-field stimulation circumvents the nonlinear processing of edges and emerging objects in BCs (Gaynes et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2022), which could potentially influence the interpretation of responses to stimuli appearing within the SAC RF (see 'Discussion).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The evolutionary algorithm training process involved iterative selection and mutation steps.
source: The evolutionary algorithm training process involved iterative selection and mutation steps. Each generation included candidate solutions for bipolar RF templates (top row) that were integrated into SAC dendrites (middle row) and ranked based on the directionality and amplitude of calcium signals (bottom row). The best solutions underwent mutation and were propagated to the next generation.
evidence: Description of the computational method shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The model was trained on five velocities.
source: The model was trained on five velocities (top, units: mm/s).
evidence: Description of the training protocol shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The evolutionary algorithm achieved a mean DSI of 37 ± 3% across all velocities.
source: Whole-cell integration of these inputs in the SAC resulted in a significant directional preference (DSI across all velocities was 37 ± 3%, Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by data from evolutionary algorithm training shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Models solely rewarded based on DSI levels often evolved strategies that aimed to minimize voltage and calcium levels.
source: Models solely rewarded based on DSI levels often evolved strategies that aimed to minimize voltage and calcium levels. This effect was most evident at slow stimulation speeds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data from alternative model training shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Physiological somatic excitatory currents and dendritic calcium responses in SACs exhibit consistent peak levels across the velocity spectrum.
source: In contrast to the predictions of the threshold-based strategy, physiological somatic excitatory currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and dendritic calcium responses in SACs exhibit consistent peak levels across the velocity spectrum (Ding et al., 2016; Koren et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The performance of the threshold-based approach, as measured by DSI, only marginally surpassed the standard configuration.
source: Furthermore, the performance of the threshold-based approach, as measured by DSI, only marginally surpassed the standard configuration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Models in which proximal and distal BCs differed only in their response delay showed DSI levels of 29 ± 2%.
source: Consistent with this, models in which proximal and distal BCs differed only in their response delay or decay times showed DSI levels close to those observed in the full model (29 ± 2% and 35 ± 3%, respectively, Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data from constrained model training shown in Figure 3.

claim: Models in which proximal and distal BCs differed only in their decay times showed DSI levels of 35 ± 3%.
source: Consistent with this, models in which proximal and distal BCs differed only in their response delay or decay times showed DSI levels close to those observed in the full model (29 ± 2% and 35 ± 3%, respectively, Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data from constrained model training shown in Figure 3.

claim: The optimal solutions in the full model evolved toward larger RF centers in the distal BCs (42 ± 15 µm vs. 32 ± 9 µm).
source: In line with this observation, the optimal solutions in the full model evolved toward larger RF centers in the distal BCs (42 ± 15 µm vs. 32 ± 9 µm, Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data from evolutionary algorithm training shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When center width was the only varying RF parameter, the difference in RF size was more pronounced (97 ± 18 µm vs. 22 ± 3 µm).
source: The difference in RF size was more pronounced when center width was the only varying RF parameter (97 ± 18 µm vs. 22 ± 3 µm), resulting in a measurable lag (approximately 135 ms for stimulus velocity = 0.5 mm/s, Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data from constrained model training shown in Figure 3.

claim: The impact of spatial RF properties on directional tuning managed to elevate the DS by about twofold over the space-invariant configuration (DSI = 19 ± 4%).
source: The impact of spatial RF properties on directional tuning was not as pronounced as the temporal RF characteristics but managed to elevate the DS by about twofold over the space-invariant configuration (DSI = 19 ± 4%, p<10–11 vs. identical BCs, Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data from constrained model training shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Despite variations in perisomatic electrical properties, all models generated by the EA achieved comparable DS levels.
source: Despite these variations in perisomatic electrical properties, all models generated by the EA achieved comparable DS levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by data from models with varying compartmentalization shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The effectiveness of the space-time wiring model relies primarily on BC kinetics, which are influenced by the spatiotemporal properties of their RF organization.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the effectiveness of the space-time wiring model relies primarily on BC kinetics, which are influenced by the spatiotemporal properties of their RF organization.
evidence: Inference from simulation results.

claim: The specific details of postsynaptic integration appear to play a lesser role in the space-time wiring DS mechanism.
source: In contrast, the specific details of postsynaptic integration appear to play a lesser role in this DS mechanism.
evidence: Inference from simulation results.

claim: Floxed iGluSnFR was virally expressed in ChAT-Cre mice to specifically target ON- and OFF-SACs.
source: To specifically target ON- and OFF-SACs, we virally expressed floxed iGluSnFR in ChAT-Cre mice (Figure 5).
evidence: Description of experimental method shown in Figure 5.

claim: Experiments were performed 3–6 weeks after vector introduction.
source: Then, 3–6 wk after vector introduction, we performed ex vivo experiments using a whole-mount retina preparation.
evidence: Description of experimental timeline.

claim: Visual stimuli consisted of full-field flashes and bars moving at five different velocities.
source: Visual stimuli consisted of full-field flashes and bars moving alternatively either from left to right or in the opposite direction at five different velocities (Figure 5B) and oriented bars used to map RFs using the filtered back-projection approach (Figure 5C).
evidence: Description of experimental stimuli shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Hierarchical clustering identified seven functional groups for the ON-SAC population.
source: The analysis identified seven groups for the ON-SAC population (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and six for the OFF-SACs (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) as providing the optimal separation (Franke et al., 2017; Gaynes et al., 2022; Matsumoto et al., 2021; Matsumoto et al., 2019; Rasmussen et al., 2020; Strauss et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by data from hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hierarchical clustering identified six functional groups for the OFF-SAC population.
source: The analysis identified seven groups for the ON-SAC population (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and six for the OFF-SACs (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) as providing the optimal separation (Franke et al., 2017; Gaynes et al., 2022; Matsumoto et al., 2021; Matsumoto et al., 2019; Rasmussen et al., 2020; Strauss et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by data from hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: BC dynamics vary systematically with axonal stratification level in the IPL.
source: As BC dynamics vary systematically with axonal stratification level in the IPL (Franke et al., 2017), we sorted the functional clusters based on their transiency of the response dynamics, with C1 representing the most transient shape (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study and data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Functional clusters with the longest lags in response to flashes tended to respond quickest to moving bars.
source: Unexpectedly, our experimental findings have uncovered a reversed relationship in the response delays (Pearson correlation coefficient, r = –0.98). Functional clusters with the longest lags in response to flashes tended to respond quickest to moving bars (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In certain clusters, negative delays in response to motion were observed, indicating that glutamate release begins before the moving bar reaches the position of the cell.
source: In certain clusters, we observed negative delays in response to motion, indicating that glutamate release begins before the moving bar reaches the position of the cell (Berry et al., 1999; Trenholm et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to prior studies.

claim: A clear relationship was discovered between the lag in response to moving stimuli and the measured RF half-width (r = –0.99).
source: Our observations supported this hypothesis as we discovered a clear relationship between the lag in response to moving stimuli and the measured RF half-width (r = –0.99, Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There is a significant difference between the activation lag following a flashed and moving stimuli.
source: Taken together, our results indicate a significant difference between the activation lag following a flashed and moving stimuli.
evidence: Inference from experimental data.

claim: The spatial properties of the RF play a significant role in determining the delay for motion responses but have no impact on the lag seen following the presentation of full-field flashes.
source: The spatial properties of the RF play a significant role in determining the delay for motion responses but have no impact on the lag seen following the presentation of full-field flashes, which engage the entire RF regardless of its size.
evidence: Inference from experimental data.

claim: The RF mapping approach was able to faithfully reproduce the empirical glutamate dynamics observed in the training dataset.
source: Using this approach, we were able to faithfully reproduce the empirical glutamate dynamics observed in the training dataset (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data from RF model training shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The simulated output reliably replicated experimental waveforms for full-field flashes, even though these stimuli were not part of the training set.
source: Encouragingly, even though these stimuli were not part of the training set, the simulated output reliably replicated experimental waveforms, despite substantially different dynamics in many clusters (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data from RF model validation shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A strong agreement was found between the rise time of the flash response and the predicted kinetics of RF centers across all functional clusters.
source: We found a strong agreement between the rise time of the flash response and the predicted kinetics of RF centers across all functional clusters (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by data from RF model validation shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Response delay in the models reliably followed the lags seen in flash responses.
source: Similarly, response delay in the models reliably followed the lags seen in flash responses (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by data from RF model validation shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The models consistently converged on narrow RFs, typically ranging from 50 to 100 µm for the majority of functional clusters.
source: Our models consistently converged on narrow RFs, typically ranging from 50 to 100 µm for the majority of functional clusters, consistent with the classical RF description for retinal BCs (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1; Euler et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2017; Kuo et al., 2016; Schwartz et al., 2012; Strauss et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2018; Wienbar and Schwartz, 2018).
evidence: Supported by data from RF model training shown in Figure 8C and citations to prior studies.

claim: The models predicted significantly more extensive RFs for ON-C1 and ON-C4, with half-widths of 379 ± 13 and 198 ± 6.7 µm, respectively.
source: Finally, in a close match with experimentally mapped RFs (Figure 7B), the models predicted significantly more extensive RFs for ON-C1 and ON-C4, with half-widths of 379 ± 13 and 198 ± 6.7 µm, respectively (Figure 8C), strongly suggesting that RF formulation derived from motion responses is accurate and could be used to predict signal processing in untrained visual conditions.
evidence: Supported by data from RF model training shown in Figure 8C.

claim: For ON-SACs, the highest DSI = 17 ± 2% was observed with inputs from ON-C6 (proximal) and ON-C2 (distal).
source: For ON-SACs, the highest DSI = 17 ± 2% was observed with inputs from ON-C6 (proximal) and ON-C2 (distal).
evidence: Supported by data from evolutionary algorithm training with experimental waveforms.

claim: In the case of OFF-SACs, the highest DSI levels (21 ± 3%) were associated with OFF-C1 and OFF-C5.
source: In the case of OFF-SACs, the inputs performed slightly better, with the highest DSI levels (21 ± 3%) associated with OFF-C1 and OFF-C5 (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by data from evolutionary algorithm training with experimental waveforms shown in Figure 9.

claim: SACs innervated by BCs with identical RF formulation had substantially lower directional capabilities (DSI = 5 ± 1% for ON-SACs and 7 ± 1% for OFF-SACs).
source: In contrast, SACs innervated by BCs with identical RF formulation had substantially lower directional capabilities (DSI = 5 ± 1% for ON-SACs and 7 ± 1% for OFF-SACs, Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by data from evolutionary algorithm training with experimental waveforms shown in Figure 9.

claim: The degree of measured DS did not exhibit a significant correlation with the extent of dendritic isolation.
source: Our observations yielded a result consistent with what we observed with synthetic BC inputs: the degree of measured DS did not exhibit a significant correlation with the extent of dendritic isolation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optimal DS was achieved in both ON and OFF circuits when two clusters dominated the proximal and distal innervation regions.
source: We observed that the simulations converged on similar solutions, irrespective of the initial randomized cluster distribution. Optimal DS was achieved in both ON and OFF circuits when two clusters dominated the proximal and distal innervation regions (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by data from evolutionary algorithm training shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The levels of DS obtained in simulations with multiple clusters did not significantly differ from the findings of the simple proximal-distal parameter exploration (ON-SACs: DSI = 17 ± 5%, OFF-SACs: DSI = 21 ± 6%).
source: Consequently, the levels of DS obtained in these simulations did not significantly differ from the findings of the simple proximal-distal parameter exploration presented earlier (ON-SACs: DSI = 17 ± 5%, OFF-SACs: DSI = 21 ± 6%, Figure 10C–F).
evidence: Supported by data from evolutionary algorithm training shown in Figure 10C-F.

claim: Optimal combination of excitatory signals has the potential to triple the level of directional tuning over SAC-intrinsic mechanisms.
source: Based on these results, we can conclude that optimal combination of excitatory signals has the potential to triple the level of directional tuning over SAC-intrinsic mechanisms (Figure 10D and F; Tukker et al., 2004; Vlasits et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: Inference from simulation results shown in Figure 10D and F, with citations to prior studies.

claim: The kinetics and RF description of distal clusters (ON-C2 and OFF-C1) were about twofold longer than the optimal synthetic distal inputs.
source: Focusing on the clusters identified by our analysis as contributing to the highest directional tuning, we note that although distal clusters (ON-C2 and OFF-C1) had the shortest duration and fastest delays, their kinetics and RF description were about twofold longer than the optimal synthetic distal inputs (Figure 11, Figure 11—figure supplement 1), with the largest difference being the rise time dynamics of ON-C2 (303 ± 110 ms vs. 45 ± 12 ms for optimal model).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental and synthetic RF parameters shown in Figure 11.

claim: The durations of ON-C6 and OFF-C5 were 1.25 ± 0.49 s/1.28 ± 0.34, respectively, compared to 0.31 ± 0.15 s measured for synthetic RFs.
source: Even further pronounced were the differences in recorded vs. optimal proximal solutions. The durations of ON-C6 and OFF-C5 were 1.25 ± 0.49 s/1.28 ± 0.34, respectively, compared to 0.31 ± 0.15 s measured for synthetic RFs.
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental and synthetic RF parameters.

claim: The transiency indexes calculated for ON-C6 and OFF-C5 were around 0.4, while optimal synthetic waveforms had TI = 0.87 ± 0.09.
source: Similarly, the transiency indexes calculated for these clusters were around 0.4, while optimal synthetic waveforms had TI = 0.87 ± 0.09 (Figure 11).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental and synthetic RF parameters shown in Figure 11.

claim: Glutamate release in the bipolar–SAC circuit has slow dynamics that can mediate substantial, albeit suboptimal, DS.
source: Thus, glutamate release in the bipolar–SAC circuit has slow dynamics that can mediate substantial, albeit suboptimal, DS.
evidence: Inference from comparison of experimental and optimal synthetic parameters.

claim: Our prior work demonstrated a low correlation between the dynamics of BC responses to motion and static stimuli.
source: The original space-time wiring hypothesis was conceptualized for individual SAC dendrites, and the difference in BC response shape was considered through the lens of the dynamics of responses to static stimuli (Kim et al., 2014). Although these circumstances were thought to simplify the analysis of dendritic computations, it is now clear that signal preprocessing in the bipolar population introduces unforeseen challenges to this approach: our prior work demonstrated a low correlation between the dynamics of BC responses to motion and static stimuli (Gaynes et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: We replicate the result of low correlation between the dynamics of BC responses to motion and static stimuli on a new dataset.
source: Here, we replicate this result on a new dataset (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), reinforcing the notion that signal kinetics, crucial to the space-time wiring model, are not a fixed property of the cell but are instead dependent on the stimulus.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Presynaptic signals can exhibit prolonged flash-lags yet generate early responses to motion, a phenomenon explained by their spatial RF structure.
source: For example, we demonstrate that presynaptic signals can exhibit prolonged flash-lags yet generate early responses to motion, a phenomenon explained by their spatial RF structure (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Stimuli that activate only a small portion of the SAC dendritic tree in isolation or all dendrites through the same stimulation pattern are likely to introduce nonlinear signal processing in BCs.
source: In addition, it is vital to consider the implications of using stimuli that activate only a small portion of the SAC dendritic tree in isolation or all dendrites through the same stimulation pattern. Such stimulus designs are likely to introduce nonlinear signal processing in BCs and, importantly, result in asymmetric bipolar responses for different stimulation directions (Gaynes et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Compartmentalization has little effect on directional tuning produced by the space-time wiring model.
source: Interestingly, our results demonstrate that in contrast to these postsynaptic mechanisms, compartmentalization has little effect on directional tuning produced by the space-time wiring model (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data from simulations with varying compartmentalization shown in Figure 4.

claim: EAs have broad applicability and have been successfully utilized in examining the mechanisms of directional computations of SACs before.
source: EAs have broad applicability and have been successfully utilized in examining the mechanisms of directional computations of SACs before (Ezra-Tsur et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Our largest model, which consisted of 23 free parameters, consistently evolved toward similar solutions regardless of the starting parameters.
source: While they may be susceptible to getting trapped in local minima, our largest model, which consisted of 23 free parameters (9 × 2 presynaptic + 5 postsynaptic, as described in 'Methods'), consistently evolved toward similar solutions regardless of the starting parameters.
evidence: Description of model performance.

claim: We present a novel application of model fitting to map RFs based on responses to moving stimuli.
source: We present a novel application of model fitting to map RFs based on responses to moving stimuli.
evidence: Description of methodological contribution.

claim: Our study did not specifically investigate the measurement of directional release from individual axonal terminals.
source: In particular, our study did not specifically investigate the measurement of directional release from individual axonal terminals, as previously demonstrated in type 2 and 7 BCs that innervate OFF- and ON-SACs (Matsumoto et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement of limitation with citation to prior study.

claim: We attribute the lack of detection of directionally tuned release sites to the sparsity of these sites, which are overshadowed by the release from non-directionally tuned units.
source: We attribute this result to the sparsity of the directionally tuned release sites, which are overshadowed by the release from non-directionally tuned units.
evidence: Speculation about the reason for not detecting directionally tuned release.

claim: It is presently unknown whether the contacts made by DS boutons on SACs are aligned with the soma-dendritic tip axis to enhance DS in the outward direction.
source: In addition, it is presently unknown whether the contacts made by DS boutons on SACs are aligned with the soma-dendritic tip axis to enhance DS in the outward direction (Srivastava et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement of uncertainty with citation.

claim: We were intrigued by the discovery of presynaptic cells exhibiting broad RFs that spanned hundreds of microns.
source: We were intrigued by the discovery of presynaptic cells exhibiting broad RFs that spanned hundreds of microns.
evidence: Description of experimental finding.

claim: Our findings bear a resemblance to a recent study that described elongated RFs in type 5A BCs.
source: Our findings bear a resemblance to a recent study that described elongated RFs in type 5A BCs (Hanson et al., 2023), challenging the classical understanding of bipolar RF structure, which suggests that the extent of the center component is limited to the size of their dendritic fields, typically below 50 µm in the mouse (Euler et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2017; Gaynes et al., 2022; Kuo et al., 2016; Schwartz et al., 2012; Strauss et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2018; Wienbar and Schwartz, 2018), but see Asari and Meister, 2012 for an example of large bipolar RFs in the salamander.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: One plausible mechanistic explanation for the observed extensive RFs is the presence of gap-junction coupling among neighboring BCs.
source: One plausible mechanistic explanation for the observed extensive RFs is the presence of gap-junction coupling among neighboring BCs (Kuo et al., 2016), which could be part of the adaptive changes in the bipolar–SAC circuits to repeated stimulation (Ankri et al., 2020; Vlasits et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The number of functional clusters observed in our dataset exceeds the number of BC subtypes known to connect to SACs in the mouse (five OFF and four ON types).
source: If correct, the mechanism could explain why the number of functional clusters observed in our dataset exceeds the number of BC subtypes known to connect to SACs in the mouse (five OFF and four ON types, Ding et al., 2016; Greene et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison of experimental findings to known anatomy, with citations.

claim: While most functional clusters were observed in multiple recording sessions, some clusters were observed more rarely.
source: In line with this interpretation, while most functional clusters were observed in multiple recording sessions, some clusters were observed more rarely (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) – perhaps due to differently adapted state of the retina in these preparations.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Another potential explanation for the abundant functional classes observed in our recordings is the possibility of glutamate release originating from amacrine cells.
source: Another potential explanation for the abundant functional classes observed in our recordings is the possibility of glutamate release originating from amacrine cells (Grimes et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Glutamatergic amacrine cells typically do not establish direct synapses with SACs.
source: It is worth noting that, to the best of our knowledge, glutamatergic amacrine cells typically do not establish direct synapses with SACs.
evidence: Statement based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Glutamatergic amacrine cells release glutamate in close proximity to ON-SAC dendrites.
source: However, these cells release glutamate in close proximity to ON-SAC dendrites (Mani et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Glutamatergic amacrine cells are known to exhibit a small center region and pronounced surrounds.
source: Glutamatergic amacrine cells are known to exhibit a small center region and pronounced surrounds (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Mouse SACs exhibit spatial preference to different presynaptic bipolar types.
source: Mouse SACs exhibit spatial preference to different presynaptic bipolar types (Ding et al., 2016; Greene et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: This spatial separation is not absolute, especially in ON-SACs, where most dendritic regions may receive input from multiple presynaptic cell types.
source: However, this spatial separation is not absolute, especially in ON-SACs, where most dendritic regions may receive input from multiple presynaptic cell types.
evidence: Statement based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The space-time wiring model's effectiveness in conveying directional performance diminishes when a clear boundary does not exist between proximally and distally innervating presynaptic populations.
source: The space-time wiring model's effectiveness in conveying directional performance diminishes when a clear boundary does not exist between proximally and distally innervating presynaptic populations (Figure 10).
evidence: Inference from simulation results shown in Figure 10.

claim: We intentionally did not impose a strict match between the synaptic distribution in our model and biological data.
source: It is important to note that we intentionally did not impose a strict match between the synaptic distribution in our model and biological data.
evidence: Description of modeling approach.

claim: Our findings establish an upper limit on the contribution of the space-time wiring mechanism to SAC directional tuning.
source: As a result, our findings establish an upper limit on the contribution of the space-time wiring mechanism to SAC directional tuning.
evidence: Inference from modeling approach.

claim: We observed a slightly higher DS in the OFF population, consistent with a previous study.
source: While we observed a slightly higher DS in the OFF population, consistent with a previous study (Fransen and Borghuis, 2017), our investigation reveals that the waveforms produced by presynaptic cells in response to moving objects do not fully exploit the potential for directional tuning that can be achieved with synthetic BCs, as depicted in Figures 2 and 10.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 10, with citation to prior study.

claim: The DS levels we project for experimentally recorded glutamate signals exhibit 30-50% enhancement compared to the directional performance of a space-time wiring model observed in a recent study by Srivastava et al., 2022.
source: It is worth highlighting that the DS levels we project for experimentally recorded glutamate signals exhibit 30-50% enhancement compared to the directional performance of a space-time wiring model observed in a recent study by Srivastava et al., 2022
evidence: Comparison to prior study.

claim: The primary distinction between our study and Srivastava et al., 2022 likely arises from the fact that Srivastava et al., 2022 investigated flash-evoked glutamate waveforms while we integrated over responses to moving stimuli.
source: The primary distinction between our studies likely arises from the fact that Srivastava et al., 2022 investigated flash-evoked glutamate waveforms. In contrast, we integrated over responses to moving stimuli.
evidence: Comparison of methodological approaches.

claim: Motion responses within the bipolar population offer a more suitable foundation for achieving directional tuning than flash responses.
source: This discrepancy suggests that, while suboptimal, motion responses within the bipolar population still offer a more suitable foundation for achieving directional tuning.
evidence: Inference from comparison of results.

claim: Wu et al., 2023 put forward the idea that the spatial arrangement of midget and DB4/5 BCs in the primate retina might contribute to DS computation through a similar space-time wiring mechanism.
source: Notably, Wu et al., 2023 put forward the idea that the spatial arrangement of midget and DB4/5 BCs in the primate retina might contribute to DS computation through a similar space-time wiring mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: If primate BCs exhibit faster dynamics than those observed in mice, the space-time wiring model's influence on SAC function in primates may be even more pronounced.
source: While we lack information regarding the exact shapes of motion responses in primate BCs, it is reasonable to speculate that if they exhibit faster dynamics than those observed in mice, the space-time wiring model's influence on SAC function in primates may be even more pronounced.
evidence: Speculation about cross-species differences.

claim: Additional mechanisms are necessary to account for the observed DS capabilities in a manner consistent with empirical evidence.
source: These results strongly indicate that additional mechanisms are necessary to account for the observed DS capabilities in a manner consistent with empirical evidence.
evidence: Inference from comparison of model predictions to experimental observations.

source: SACs possess intricate morphologies and express multiple voltage-gated channels (Morrie and Feller, 2018; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

source: These cells are integral components of complex neural circuits, the architectural details of which remain incompletely understood but allow SACs to convey functionally distinct signals to postsynaptic targets (Pottackal et al., 2021; Sethuramanujam et al., 2021).
